question: Did Jesus oppose the sacrifice system?
subtitle: And the vegetarian question, honestly
aliases: did Jesus eat lamb at Passover
finding: Jesus stood in the Hebrew prophetic tradition that rejected animal sacrifice as something God never asked for, and he said so, twice, quoting Hosea. His single most dramatic public act was shutting down the sacrificial economy inside the Temple while quoting the one chapter in Jeremiah where God denies ever commanding burnt offerings. That action is what got him killed. His family and community carried the same position: his brother James ate no meat and drank no wine, and the Nazarene-Ebionite successors held that meat-eating and sacrifice were unlawful. We do not claim certainty about what was on Jesus's plate. We claim the anti-sacrifice position is documented, inherited and central, and that reading his death as the blood sacrifice God required inverts the thing he spent his ministry opposing. Scope control: our claim is about where he located God's requirement, not that he never touched the institutions of his own society.
oneLiners: He said "I desire mercy, not sacrifice," and then he walked into the Temple and let the animals out. That's not a metaphor, that's a policy.
He quoted the one chapter in the Bible where God denies ever asking for sacrifice. Then they decided to kill him. Those two facts are in the same paragraph of Mark.
His brother ate no meat and drank no wine, from birth, per Hegesippus. Same house, same parents, same tradition.
A scribe told him love was worth more than every burnt offering in the Temple. Jesus told him he was close to the kingdom. He didn't say "close, but."
Yes, he sent the leper to the priest; that's how a quarantined man got his life back. Then read Matthew 5:24: leave the gift at the altar and go make peace first. The offering is the part that waits.
doNotSay: "Hosea 6:6 is not a comparison." The second line is "more than burnt offerings." Anyone with a Hebrew Bible open will correct you.
Don't run the thuō lexical argument from John 10:10. In Koine, thuō routinely means plain slaughter (Luke 15:23, Acts 10:13, Luke 22:7). Keep the literary reversal, drop the lexicon.

Don't call the "I have no desire to eat the flesh of this Passover" line the Hebrew Matthew used by Jesus's own community. It is Epiphanius quoting the Ebionites' alteration of Luke 22:15 (Panarion 30.22.4). Good evidence of what James's successors believed; not evidence of what Jesus said.
"Qumran was anti-sacrifice." It wasn't. Let the scrolls establish the context, not the thesis; the thesis rests on the prophets.
"The Didache has no sacrifice." Chapter 14 does, of the assembly's own offering. Claim the prayers, not the whole document.

sources.phrase: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice
sources.note: "Go ye and learn what that meaneth" is a rabbinic rebuke: you have fundamentally misread scripture. Aimed at the men running the cult.
The second time, in a Sabbath dispute. He isn't citing Hosea to reform sacrifice; he's citing it to overrule them.
The verse itself, with its second line. Say the Hebrew carefully: 6:6a a flat "not," 6:6b "more than."

He drove out the sheep and the oxen: the sacrificial animals, released. The detail is John's, and John relocated the event to the start of the ministry; the anti-sacrifice reading survives on Mark 11 plus Jeremiah 7 without it. Say so.

sources.phrase: carry any vessel through the temple
sources.note: He blocked the flow of goods through the court, explained himself with Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, and in the next breath "the chief priests and the scribes... sought how they might destroy him" (11:18).

sources.phrase: I spake not unto your fathers
sources.note: The chapter he quoted in the Temple: "I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them... concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices." Nobody reaches for Jeremiah 7 to complain about currency fees.

sources.phrase: more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices
sources.note: The cleanest red-text datum and rarely quoted. A scribe states the prophetic position out loud; Jesus does not correct or qualify him: "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God."

sources.title: Didache 9-10, the earliest communion prayers
sources.note: Thanks for a lineage and for knowledge. No body, no blood, no death. Compare the cup saying's manuscript record: Mark 14:24 has "shed for many"; Matthew 26:28 alone adds "for the remission of sins."

sources.phrase: Leave there thy gift before the altar
sources.note: Yes, it assumes an altar. The instruction is to walk away mid-sacrifice and reconcile first. The offering is the thing that gets interrupted. Hosea 6:6 turned into a procedure.

sources.tier: red text · triple-attested · the strongest counter-evidence
sources.phrase: offer the gift that Moses commanded
sources.note: "Jesus commands a Temple sacrifice." Name it as the strongest counter-evidence. One: the thesis it refutes isn't ours; Jeremiah preached 7:22 in the Temple gate. Two: the Leviticus 14 offering is the certification procedure by which a quarantined man gets his civic life back, "for a testimony unto them." Three: Matthew 5:23-24 cuts our way. Four: Luke 2:22-24 is his parents' offering; he kept Passover and no gospel narrates him eating the lamb.

sources.phrase: a piece of a broiled fish
sources.note: "Jesus ate fish." We don't need a vegetarian Jesus for the anti-sacrifice case and don't claim certainty about his diet. When he explains the feeding miracles he mentions only the loaves (Mark 8:19-21); Luke 24:42 is textually unstable (some manuscripts add a honeycomb); the Syriac Peshitta at Luke 21:34 reads "eating of flesh."

"He kept Passover, so he ate the lamb; and he's the Lamb of God." No gospel narrates him eating lamb. What all three Synoptics narrate is a substitution: bread and wine at the central sacrificial meal, the Melchizedek pattern (Genesis 14:18). "Lamb of God" is the Fourth Gospel's framing, not a red-text self-description. The Ebionite inversion of this verse (Panarion 30.22.4) shows what James's successors believed he taught.

sources.phrase: not come to destroy, but to fulfil
sources.note: "The Law commands sacrifice; he came to fulfill it." The prophets got there first: Jeremiah 7:22, Isaiah 1:12 ("who hath required this at your hand?"), Isaiah 66:3, Psalm 51:16, Amos 5:25, Micah 6:8; and Jeremiah 8:8 names the mechanism. Jesus affirming the Law and rejecting the cult is exactly the prophetic position, the one he endorsed in Mark 12:33-34, and the one the Clementine Homilies systematized (2.38).

sources.tier: Dead Sea Scrolls · our own file
sources.title: The Temple Scroll and 4QMMT prescribe sacrifice
sources.note: "Qumran wasn't anti-sacrifice." Correct. What Qumran gives us is narrower: documentary proof that a literate priestly movement judged the operating Temple's sacrifices invalid, withdrew, and substituted prayer and right conduct (1QS 3:4-7; 8:12-14). Our claim that God never commanded sacrifice rests on the prophets, not the scrolls.

sources.note: "He drank no wine or strong drink, nor did he eat meat," from his mother's womb. Same household, same tradition. Reference level until the text is held.

sources.title: Eusebius, Demonstratio Evangelica 3.5
sources.edition: Ferrar (1920), public domain in the US; not yet held
sources.note: "The twelve apostles embraced abstinence from wine and meat." Cited at chapter level (3.5); paraphrase until held.

sources.title: Epiphanius, Panarion 18 and 29, the Nasaraeans and Nazoraeans
sources.note: "In their eyes it was unlawful to eat meat or make sacrifices with it" (Panarion 18). Keep Panarion 18 (pre-Christian Nasaraeans) and 29 (Nazoraeans) distinct. Then Canon 14 of Ancyra (314 CE) had to order clergy who abstained from flesh to at least taste it; councils don't legislate against rare behavior.
